Engraven
en-GRAY-vn
v. (cut into a hard surface; incised)
Greek entupoo, to impress or stamp in. The Authorized Version uses the older strong participle engraven rather than engraved, and the word appears once, of the law cut into stone at Sinai.

Biblical Definition

But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away. Paul is arguing from the lesser to the greater, and the whole force of the argument sits on the word engraven. The law was cut into stone — permanent, external, unyielding, and given with such glory that Moses' face had to be veiled. Paul grants all of it. He calls that ministration glorious, twice. But he calls it the ministration of death, because a perfect standard cut in stone can only condemn a heart that is not made of the same material. The contrast is not between a bad covenant and a good one but between a glory that fades and a glory that remains. Against the tables of stone Paul sets the epistle of Christ, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart — the very thing Jeremiah had promised when the Lord said, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts. The law is not abolished in the new covenant. It changes surface. What was engraven on stone outside the man is inscribed by the Spirit within him.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): cut, as letters or figures, on a hard substance; imprinted; deeply impressed.

expand to see more

ENGRAVE, v.t. To cut, as metals, stones or other hard substances, with a chisel or graver; to cut figures, letters or devices on stone or metal.

ENGRAVEN, pp. Cut, as figures or letters, on a hard substance; imprinted.

ENGRAVE, v.t. To imprint; to impress deeply; to infix.

GRAVEN, pp. Cut or engraved; carved; sculptured.

TABLE, n. A flat surface of wood, stone or metal, on which anything is written or engraved; as the tables of the law.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 3:7 — "But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away:"

2 Corinthians 3:3 — "Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart."

Exodus 32:16 — "And the tables were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, graven upon the tables."

Jeremiah 31:33 — "But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people."

Modern Corruption

The passage is regularly made to teach that the moral law is abolished in Christ; Paul teaches that its glory is surpassed and its location moved, from stone outside the man to the heart within him.

expand to see more

Antinomian readings take the ministration of death and done away as a verdict on the law itself, concluding that the Christian is done with the commandments. The text does not permit it. Paul calls that ministration glorious, and Exodus tells us the writing was the writing of God. What is done away is the fading glory of a covenant administration, not the righteousness the law expresses. Jeremiah settles the matter from the other side: the new covenant is precisely the covenant in which God writes my law in their hearts. A new covenant that abolished the law would have nothing left to write.

The opposite error is to read the engraving as merely external still — to keep the law on stone, so to speak, and set the Christian to copying it by his own strength. That is the religion of the veiled face, and it produces either despair or self-deceit. Paul's contrast is not law against no-law but ink against Spirit, stone against flesh. The Reformed doctrine of the third use of the law holds both: the law remains the rule of the Christian's life, and the Spirit writes it where it can be obeyed, in a heart made new.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek entupoo (G1795), to engrave or stamp in; diakonia (G1248), ministration; doxa (G1391), glory; Hebrew charath (H2801), to cut in or engrave.

expand to see more

Greek entupoo (G1795) — to impress or cut in; rendered engraven, its only occurrence.

Greek diakonia (G1248) — service, ministration; used of both covenant administrations in this chapter.

Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render inoperative, to do away; of the fading glory, not of the law.

Hebrew charath (H2801) — to cut in, to engrave; used of the writing of God upon the tables.

Greek plax (G4109) — a flat tablet; set against fleshy tables of the heart.

Usage

"“written and engraven in stones” — the law cut where it could not be altered."

"“the writing was the writing of God” — the engraver named at Sinai."

"“write it in their hearts” — the promised change of surface."
